To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we report the case of a novel mutation of HADH gene in a patient presenting with HI, and we show that PET/CT scanning is an important tool for the differential diagnosis between the focal and diffuse form of HI.

(1) 18-fluorodihydroxyphenylalanin PET/CT scanning is a useful tool for distinguishing the histopathologic forms in HI, (2) the absence of metabolic disorders related to organic acids, fatty acid oxidation and amino acid, and negative mutational screening of KCNJ11 and ABC8 genes, suggest the HADH as a possible candidate gene for the diffuse form of HI.

the diffuse form of congenital hyperin-sulinism can be identified by 18-fluro-l-3, 4-dihydroxyphenylalanin positron emission tomograpy/computed tomography in patients carrying mutations of the HADDH gene, even when no metabolic disorders related to organic acids, fatty acids and amino acids are found.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of a new mutation of the HADDH gene, which is the first reported in a patient with a diffuse form of HI.

the identification of a diffuse form HI by PET/CT in a newborn carrying a novel mutation in the HADH, and with the importance of a careful metabolic investigation of the patient to identify the genetic defect.
the identification of a diffuse form in HI by PET/CT and the characterization of a novel mutation in the HADH.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presence of the diffuse form of hyperplastic islet disease should be suspected in patients with severe HI and autosomal inheritance and negative mutational screening of KCNJ11 and/or ABCC8 gene.

PET/CT scanning is a useful tool for the differential diagnosis between focal and diffuse forms of congenital hyperinulinemia, and HADH gene analysis is recommended for patients with diffuse form, even in the presence of normal acylcarnintine and organic acid profiles.
, in the absence of mutations in ABCC8 and KCNJ11 genes, a diffuse form of HI should be suspected in the presence of a positive family history and a positive PET/CT scan.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the identification of diffuse HI form by 18F-L-DOPA-PET/CT in a hyperinsulinemic patient with negative screening of KCNJ11 and/or ABCC8 genes should prompt the search for mutations of the HDAH gene, even in absence of metabolic abnormalities related to organic acids and acilcarnitines concentrations.
the use of PET/CT scanning and molecular analysis of HADH gene can be helpful in the diagnosis of patients presenting with HI and in the identification of a novel mutation in the gene.
in HI patients with negative screening for KCNJ11 and/or ABCC8 mutations, the HADH mutation should be considered as a possible cause of disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, when the diagnosis of HI is suspected, a PET/CT scan with 18-flouro-L-3, 4 dihydroxy-phenylalanine should be performed, even in patients without metabolic abnormalities.
PET/CT scanning with 18-FDOPA is able to detect diffuse HI, which is not possible by other diagnostic methods, and that the HADH mutation can be found in patients without organic acidemia.

, in a case of severe HI in a child with negative genetic testing for the most common HI genes, HADH gene mutation should be sought, and PET/CT scanning is useful in distinguishing focal and diffuse forms of the disease.
